_min_savings_comment: A listing must clear BOTH discount_threshold_pct (relative) AND min_savings_dollars (absolute) to get flagged. The dollar floor exists to keep trivial deals out, but it was set at $10, which silently excluded the entire cheap end of the hobby: a $4 card worth $12 is 67% off and saves $8, and was being rejected. Lowered to $3, with the anti-junk job moved to cheap_cards below, where it belongs -- being cheap is not the same as being junk, and a dollar floor cannot tell the difference. Ranking in the email is by dollar amount saved, highest first, so cheap finds sort to the bottom naturally and never crowd out real money.

ebay._comment: Browse API settings, used only when EBAY_CLIENT_ID/EBAY_CLIENT_SECRET are set; it then runs ALONGSIDE the alert emails and both feed the same comp corpus (an item both see is kept once, API copy). category_id 261328 is 'Trading Card Singles' under Sports Trading Cards (confirmed via scripts/lookup_ebay_category 2026-10-15). The old 212 is the parent category and also returns lots, sealed boxes and price guides, which crowd the per-call cap and can never be comps. active_listing_limit_per_player is the page size (Browse max 200). Two passes per player: newest_pages_per_player pages sorted newest first, then auction_pages_per_player pages of auctions ending soonest. 21 players x 2 calls = 42 calls a run, well inside Browse's default 5,000 a day. newest_pages_per_player starts at 1 on purpose: every new fixed-price listing becomes a corpus row, the corpus is committed to GitHub daily, and GitHub refuses files over 100MB (the email warns at 40MB). If the email warns that a player hit the newest-listing cap, raise it one page at a time and watch the corpus size line.
ebay._newest_min_price_comment: Item-price floor (USD) on the newest-first pass only; the auction pass keeps every price. Measured 2026-10-16: 77% of a newest page was under $20, a band where no flip clears economics.min_net_profit, so it filled the 200-item page (hiding the rest of the day's new listings) and grew the corpus about 3,000 rows a day. Cheaper cards still arrive through the alert emails and auctions. null = no floor.
ebay._insights_comment: Marketplace Insights (real sold prices) returned 404 for this app on 2026-10-15: limited release, not granted. Left off so a run doesn't make a wasted call per player. Set true only after eBay grants access.

ebay_alerts._comment: Used instead of the eBay API (declined account): reads eBay's own saved-search alert emails from your Gmail account via IMAP. Requires you to first create a saved search + email alert on eBay's site for each watchlist player -- see README 'eBay via saved-search email alerts'. VALIDATED against real alert emails -- see src/ebay_email_alerts.py.
ebay_alerts._mailbox_comment: Searches All Mail, not just Inbox, so you're free to archive alert emails (or filter them straight out of your inbox) without CardPro losing sight of them -- only actually deleting a message (emptying Trash) makes it disappear. Change only if your Gmail account uses a non-English locale where this folder has a different IMAP name.
ebay_alerts._max_age_comment: Corpus retention, in days. 45 matches valuation.stale_after_days: a bucket whose newest comp is older than that cannot declare a deal anyway, and at half_life_days 30 a 45-day-old ask already counts about a third of a fresh one. It was 90; with the Browse API recording ~3,000 rows a day the corpus would cross GitHub's 100 MB file limit (warned at 40 MB) well before then. Stored titles mean a parser fix still reaches every kept row (comps re-reads them on load).

craigslist._comment: Craigslist blocks automated scraping outright (confirmed against both headless and headed browser automation), so these just build ready-to-click search links included in the daily email instead of being fetched automatically.

valuation._comment: Comp-engine quality gates. These are the difference between a real valuation and a number that just restates the price. min_comps_required: how many comparable observations a bucket needs before it may be used at all. min_distinct_comp_dates / min_comp_span_days: how much CALENDAR SPREAD those observations need. Counting observations alone is not enough -- the daily scan records every listing it sees each morning, so six asks captured in one morning is one snapshot six listings deep, not six independent readings of a market. Hand-entered sold comps are exempt: three real sales on one day are three real transactions. half_life_days: recency weighting -- a comp this many days old counts half as much as one from today. stale_after_days: if the NEWEST comp in a bucket is older than this, the bucket may not declare a deal. max_dispersion: MAD/median above this means the comps disagree too much to trust a median. mad_threshold: outlier trim, in scaled median-absolute-deviations. require_flag_eligible_comp: when true (strongly recommended) only identity-and-grade-matched comp levels may declare a deal -- broader levels are shown as context but can never flag one, which is what stops the circular price-tier comparison that produced every false positive in v1.

economics._comment: Resale assumptions, not facts. Every one of these shows up in the report next to the profit figure so you can see what the number depends on. Tune them to how you actually sell. Rates checked 2026-10-16 against eBay help page id=4822.
economics._fees_comment: eBay's final value fee for sports trading cards (no Store) is 13.25%, but it is charged on the order total INCLUDING the buyer's sales tax. marketplace_fee_pct folds that in: 13.25 x 1.0753 = 14.25, where 7.53% is a 2026 average combined US sales tax (ASSUMPTION; your buyers' real rate varies by state). Per-order fee: marketplace_fixed_fee $0.40 on an order over small_order_max ($10), small_order_fixed_fee $0.30 at or under it.
economics._shipping_comment: Ship-out by method. A RAW card selling under envelope_max_sale ($20) goes by eBay Standard Envelope at envelope_shipping $0.82; everything else (raw at $20+, any slab) goes in a tracked bubble mailer at outbound_shipping $6.00 (ASSUMPTION: typical eBay-label Ground Advantage, 4 oz). supplies is per raw card ($0.50), supplies_graded per slab ($1.00) (owner ASSUMPTION).
economics._tax_comment: sales_tax_pct is what YOU pay buying: 10.25% is Chicago's combined rate, inferred from craigslist.site=chicago (ASSUMPTION; set your own). assumed_inbound_shipping is put into the money math (profit, max bid) when a listing does not state its shipping; the card still reads as shipping-unknown. $4.50 is a typical seller-charged tracked shipment (ASSUMPTION). $0 made every such card look $4-5 better than it is.
economics._haircut_comment: The gap between the median comp and what you'd realistically get selling promptly, by what the comps are. resale_haircut_asking_pct 20 applies when the comps are ASKING prices -- every comp today -- because an ask is a ceiling on what sells: measured P25/median ask is 0.79 across 44 raw buckets, so selling at the cheap end of the asks means ~20% under the median (ASSUMPTION that sales land there). resale_haircut_pct 5 applies when the comps are SOLD prices.
economics._min_net_profit_comment: The deal gate's last check: an opportunity must ALSO net at least min_net_profit after every cost above (fees, postage, supplies, purchase tax, assumed inbound shipping, haircut). $15 is the owner's floor for a buy-and-resell flip, raw or slab (ASSUMPTION). The owner's $40 floor for grade-and-flip would apply only to a grading branch, and CardPro has none, so it is not used.
economics._min_net_profit_pct_comment: The floor also scales with the card: required net = max(min_net_profit, min_net_profit_pct_of_value x estimated market value). A flat $15 is fine on a $60 card and nothing on a $1,000 one, where a 1.5% margin is inside the error of any comp, so a $1,000 card needs $100 net. Applies to the deal gate and to every MAX price (owner ASSUMPTION).
economics._minutes_per_flip_comment: Owner time per flip, for the $/h figure on each deal: 10 minutes to buy plus 15 to list, pack and ship (owner ASSUMPTION). Display only; nothing gates on it.

auctions._comment: An auction's current bid is not a price. Auctions get their own report section and their own math: the max bid is the highest you could bid and still net economics.min_net_profit at the haircut sale price, after fees, postage, supplies, tax and inbound shipping -- the same number fixed-price listings show as their max offer/buy. required_margin_pct is an optional EXTRA floor for auctions only (profit of at least that % of market value, whichever is more); it was 25, which on top of the 20% asking haircut double-counted the safety margin and put the ceiling far below what the deal gate itself accepts (ASSUMPTION: the haircut is enough). ending_soon_hours controls what counts as urgent -- only used for ordering the section, never for relaxing any quality gate.

alerts._comment: Immediate-alert tier. Deliberately conservative: too many alerts destroy the product. An opportunity must clear BOTH of these AND have a flag-eligible comp to earn an out-of-band alert -- and the dollar figure must be met by expected NET profit too, not just by the gross saving, since the gross saving ignores fees and postage; everything else waits for the morning digest. The dollar figure is 25, not the 150 it was: with focus.price_ceiling at $40 a card cannot save $150 without being worth $190, so a $150 bar meant ACT NOW could never fire on the cards this report is now built around, and an alert tier that cannot fire is not conservative, it is off. Retune this whenever you move focus.price_ceiling -- the two numbers only make sense together.

focus._comment: What reaches the email, and how long it may be. Separate from the deal gate on purpose: the gate decides whether a card is underpriced, this decides whether it is what you shop for. price_ceiling is the cheap end you actually buy and bid at; a dearer card is not called bad, it just has to be exceptional (exceptional_min_discount_pct AND exceptional_min_savings_dollars, off a flag-eligible comp) to take a slot from the cheap ones. Cards on your target list ignore BOTH price rules -- the ceiling and the bidding-room rule -- because you named those cards and set their price yourself, and a target buy_zone normally sits well above the resale-margin ceiling max_rational_bid computes. Never seeing the card you asked for is an invisible failure; a slightly longer email is a visible one. The length cap still applies to targets. require_auction_bidding_room drops auctions already bid past your max rational bid: you cannot win those at a price that works, and they cost the same space as a live one (auctions with no market value have no ceiling to be past, so they stay). max_listings caps the whole email; max_per_section is the first-pass share each section gets before the leftovers are handed out, which is what stops a 40-opportunity morning from printing zero auctions. Nothing dropped here is dropped silently -- the counts and the setting that would bring each group back are printed in the report footer. cool_cards_price_ceiling is a HIGHER ceiling that applies only to cards with something genuinely scarce about them -- a signature or a patch or a serial number -- because "is this the cheap end I shop at" and "is this a card worth looking at" are different questions and a $60 auto fails the first while passing the second. Set enabled=false for the old everything-every-day report. price_ceiling is measured against what LEAVES YOUR ACCOUNT -- item price plus known shipping plus the economics.sales_tax_pct rate -- so it means the same thing as the cost the deal gate and the profit figures are computed from, except that the gate also adds economics.assumed_inbound_shipping when shipping is unknown. At the shipped sales_tax_pct of 10.25 a $50 ceiling is about $45.35 before tax.
focus._numbered_comment: Cards numbered at or under numbered_max_print_run and costing at or under numbered_price_ceiling (item + shipping + tax) always reach the email, whatever price_ceiling says. You collect /99-or-less; in the corpus those ask a median $100, so the $40 ceiling alone hid three quarters of them. $200 covers about two thirds. Set numbered_max_print_run to 0 to switch off.
focus._deal_capital_comment: An opportunity (a deal that cleared economics.min_net_profit) reaches the email up to deal_capital_ceiling all-in (item + shipping + tax), whatever price_ceiling says. price_ceiling keeps browsing short, but it also hid the only listings that make money: fees and postage mean a $15 net almost never comes from a card under $50. $150 is a capital cap for the spending freeze through 2026 (owner ASSUMPTION). Set 0 to switch off.

cheap_cards._comment: Rules that apply only below price_ceiling. Cheap cards need their own gate because 48% of everything CardPro observes is under $10 and most of it is commodity -- base veterans, junk-wax commons, team cards. A 60%-off base common is still a base common. So a cheap card must clear a HIGHER percentage bar (min_discount_pct) and, if require_desirable_attribute is on, must actually have something that makes a copy scarce: rookie, autograph, patch/relic, serial numbering, a non-base parallel, or a grade. Anything cheap with none of those is rejected as common_card and counted in the report footer, not silently dropped. Set enabled=false to apply the ordinary rules at every price.

sold_comps._comment: Hand-entered sold prices -- the only real market data CardPro can get. Every other comp in the system is an ASKING price (a seller's opinion), which is why the engine caps those below 'high' confidence. There is no free, automatable, ToS-respecting sold-price feed: eBay's Marketplace Insights API is closed to new users, Terapeak is manual-only, and scraping breaches terms. So you enter these by hand, usually after looking a card up on 130point.com (free, covers eBay + Goldin, includes accepted Best Offers). A handful of real sales for cards you actually care about is worth more than thousands of asking prices. Add one with: python -m scripts.add_sold_comp --help

report._comment: How the email is organised. cheap_find_ceiling is what counts as pocket change: a card at or under it, with any attribute at all that makes a copy worth having, gets a CHEAP FINDS slot. That section makes no claim that the card is underpriced -- being cheap and being underpriced are different facts and CardPro can establish the first from a title and usually cannot establish the second at all. COOL CARDS is the same idea without the price bound: shown for what the card IS, ordered by how scarce or wanted it is, with no valuation attached. Between them they are the part of the email with something in it on an ordinary day.
report._cheap_auction_comment: CHEAP AUCTIONS: the pocket-change band you actually bid in. An auction whose current bid plus shipping lands between the floor and the ceiling gets its own section, claimed BEFORE 'AUCTIONS ENDING SOON' so it is not buried under slabs ten times its price -- that section sorts by time left, where a $0.99 numbered rookie sits below whatever happens to end an hour sooner. Nothing here is a deal claim: a current bid is not a price and most of these have no comp at all. Ordered by how interesting the CARD is, then by what ends soonest, because a $2 auction is a flyer and the question is whether the card is worth two dollars of attention, not whether the clock is running out. Raise the ceiling to bid in a wider band. The floor exists because below it almost every number is an untouched opening bid, and a section of untouched opening bids is a list of every auction on eBay rather than a list of finds -- set it to 0 to include them anyway -- which is where it now effectively sits, at 0.01, because the pocket-change band you actually said you shop in starts at a penny and a floor of $0.50 was deciding otherwise on your behalf. The untouched-opening-bid worry is real but it is not this setting's job: what may reach this section at all is still decided upstream by cheap_cards.require_desirable_attribute, so a $0.01 auction gets in only when the card has a rookie, auto, patch, serial number, parallel or grade on it, and the section is capped by focus.max_per_section and ordered by how interesting the card is. Raise it back to 0.5 if penny auctions start crowding the section.
